lesson.title: When Depression Doesn't Lift: Persistent Depressive Disorder
lesson.summary: Persistent depressive disorder, formerly called dysthymia, is a chronic, lower-grade form of depression that lasts for years rather than weeks, and it can occur alongside or independently of major depressive episodes.
lesson.body:
Major depressive disorder is usually described as episodic: a person experiences a period of intense symptoms, then, with or without treatment, the episode lifts and mood returns closer to baseline. Persistent depressive disorder works differently. Instead of a sharp, severe episode, the person experiences a depressed mood on most days for a very long stretch of time: at least two years for adults, or one year for children and adolescents. During that time there can be no more than two consecutive symptom free months. The individual symptoms are often milder than those seen in a major depressive episode, but their sheer duration is what makes the disorder impairing. To meet the diagnosis, a person also needs at least two of the following while depressed: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy or fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration or difficulty making decisions, and feelings of hopelessness.

One reason this distinction matters clinically is that duration and severity are separate dimensions of a mood disorder, and persistent depressive disorder sits at an unusual point on that map: lower intensity, much longer duration. It is also possible for the two patterns to combine. A person with persistent depressive disorder can, during those years of low grade depression, develop a full major depressive episode on top of it. Clinicians sometimes call this double depression, and when the acute episode resolves, the person typically settles back into the ongoing lower level depression rather than returning to a fully symptom free baseline.

Consider someone who, since their late teens, has rarely felt genuinely well. They get through school, hold a job, maintain relationships, but describe themselves as tired, joyless, and self-critical most of the time, without ever having had a dramatic breakdown. Because nothing about their functioning looks like a crisis, and because the low mood has been present for so long, they and the people around them may simply assume this is just their personality or temperament rather than a treatable condition. This pattern, chronic but unspectacular suffering, is a common reason persistent depressive disorder goes unrecognized and untreated for years.

The DSM-5 combined what used to be called dysthymic disorder with chronic major depressive disorder under this single label, reflecting the idea that duration, not just the intensity of a given episode, is a clinically meaningful way to describe depression. Because it builds directly on the diagnostic logic of major depressive disorder (many of the same core symptoms, evaluated over a longer time window with a lower symptom threshold) understanding one helps clarify the other: they are variations on how low mood can be organized in time, not two unrelated illnesses.
